Improvement of Anaerobic Digestion of Landﬁll
Leachate by Using Coagulation-Flocculation,
Fenton’s Oxidation and Air Stripping Pretreatments
Yosr Smaoui
,a Najwa Mlaik,b Jalel Bouzid,a and Sami Sayadib
aLaboratoire Genie de l’Environnement et Ecotechnologie, Ecole Nationale d’Ingenieurs de Sfax, Universite de Sfax-Tunisie,
PB 1173, Sfax, 3038, Tunisia; smaoui_yosr@yahoo.fr (for correspondence)
bP^ole d’excellence regionale AUF, (PER-LBP), Centre de Biotechnologie de Sfax, BP 1177, Laboratoire des Bioprocedes
Environnementaux, Sfax, 3061, Tunisia
Published online 00 Month 2017 in Wiley Online Library (wileyonlinelibrary.com). DOI 10.1002/ep.12781
In Tunisia, the anaerobic digestion process is regarded as a
new alternative for the treatment of landﬁll leachate (LFL).
Raw LFL contained high amounts of organic matter, high
ammonia concentrations and low biodegradability. In order
to improve anaerobic conditions and biogas yields, pretreat-
ment using coagulation-ﬂocculation, Fenton oxidation (FO)
and air stripping processes were investigated and compared in
terms of biogas production. Air stripping process was optimized
using Response Surface Methodology (RSM). Central Composite
Design (CCD) was used with three factors. Under optimized
conditions, removals of 85% ammonia, 26% chemical oxygen
demand (COD) were achieved. Coagulation-ﬂocculation pro-
vided an increase in the efﬂuent biodegradability with 46% of
COD reduction. Fenton’s oxidation allowed reducing 48%
COD, 30% of biological oxygen demand (BOD5). The effect of
pretreatments was investigated with the biochemical methane
potential (BMP) assay. A comparison of three different pre-
treatment methods of LFL for biogas production was performed.
Air stripping was demonstrated as providing a better biogas
yield than other pretreatments which reached 588 mL/g
CODint. The best methane yield was obtained using air strip-
ping pretreatment under optimized conditions. It can result in
more robust and effective anaerobic digestion. V

INTRODUCTION
Landﬁll leachate is a contaminated liquid formed by excess
water percolating through the waste layers in landﬁlls. It con-
tains a high concentration of organic contaminants, ammonia,
salts, even heavy metals and xenobiotic organic compounds
such as phthalates [1] that can cause severe environmental
impacts by contaminating surface and ground water [2]. To
minimize these impacts, efﬁcient, environmentally and eco-
nomically viable processes for the landﬁll leachate treatment
are required.
In Tunisia, treatment of leachate stations adopts a strategy
consisting
of
a
set
of
successive
operations
that
are
coagulation-ﬂocculation followed by an aerobic membrane
bioreactor, ultraﬁltration and ﬁnally a polishing step by
reverse osmosis membranes. Tunisian LFL is characterized by
a high concentration of chemical oxygen demand (COD>
30 g/L) and ammonia nitrogen (>3 g/L), in addition to a low
biodegradability and the presence of some heavy metals.
Moreover, the high concentration of organic matter present
in Tunisian landﬁll leachate, make the treatment process
costly in terms of the frequent use of chemicals and the high
energy requirements.
The main idea of this study was to propose an alternative
approach for the treatment of a leachate generated in a con-
trolled discharge in Tunisia. Anaerobic digestion (AD), the most
popular biological treatment, produces moderate amounts of
sludge, quite effective for young leachate and generates energy
from the methane produced making this process economically
and environmentally advantageous [3,4].
Various studies showed the presence of a wide variety of
substances that are considered as inhibitors of the anaerobic
digestion process [5]. However, an obstacle for biological treat-
ment of leachate is the high ammonia concentration that can
inhibit the growth of microorganisms and deteriorate the per-
formance of the treatment. It was suggested that inhibition
might occur in the range of 1500–7000 mg/L of total ammonia
nitrogen [6]. The C/N ratio is considered as a key factor for
anaerobic digestion. In fact, if this ratio is small, which is the
case of some leachate, nitrogen is liberated, accumulates in
the form of ammonia and begins to apply a toxic effect when
the pH is higher than 8.5 [7]. Therefore, the low C/N ratio and
the poor biodegradability of landﬁll leachate reduce the
effectiveness of biological treatment processes and require
preliminary physico-chemical treatments [8].
As already mentioned, the coagulation-ﬂocculation process,
is the ﬁrst treatment used in the leachate treatment plants in
controlled discharges of Tunisia. This process is widely used
because of its easy operation, low capital and operating cost
and environmental impact [9,10].
Various studies have shown the effectiveness of this pro-
cess for pretreatment of wastewater [11,12], which reduces
pollutant loads, removes recalcitrant compounds and there-
fore, improves the biodegradability of wastewater during the
biological treatment. Selection of appropriate coagulant, the

effect of pH and investigation of the dosage of optimal
reagents are required to reach optimal performance.
Advanced Oxidation Processes (AOPs) such as ozonation,
UV/H2O2, photocatalytic oxidation are considered clean tech-
nologies for the treatment of wastewater [13]. The highly oxi-
dative hydroxyl radical (OH•) produced in this process can
oxidize refractory organic matter into more biodegradable
compounds, then improves the biodegradability of efﬂuent
that can be further treated by an economical biological pro-
cess [14,15]. Therefore, Fenton process, which is one of the
AOPs, is technologically simple, iron and hydrogen peroxide
used are not toxic and can enhance the biodegradability of
wastewater; further facilitating the following biological pro-
cess which may be more reasonable so as to avoid high
energy consumption [16]. Ammonia or air stripping is the
most widely employed treatment for the removal of NH3-N
from landﬁll leachate [17]. The concentrated gaseous ammo-
nia purged after stripping can be recovered and absorbed by
strong acidic solutions, such as sulfuric acid (H2SO4), form-
ing a mineral fertilizer for agricultural use [2]. To reduce the
cost of the process and to select the most economical param-
eters (pH, aeration rate and reaction time) that offer a suit-
able C/N ratio for the subsequent anaerobic, optimization of
the pretreatment can be a vital practice to improve the total
efﬁciency of the process. Response surface method (RSM) is
a statistical tool for optimization of different processes for
wastewater treatment. In this study, a central composite
design (CCD) was used to optimize the three factors, pH,
aeration rate and reaction time as the main factors in the air
stripping process.
The main objective of the present study was to investigate
the effect of coagulation-ﬂocculation, FO with zero valent
iron and air stripping on biodegradability and C/N ratio
improvement. The effect of these pretreatments processes on
the anaerobic digestion was investigated.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Landfill Leachate Sampling and Inocula
The leachate used in this study was obtained from a dis-
charge in the Sfax region of Tunisia. It is taken straight from
the collection box, and kept at 48C in the dark before being
used in the experiments to avoid its decomposition. The
mean physico-chemical characteristics of raw leachate are
shown in Table 1. For batch anaerobic digestion experi-
ments, the seed sludge was taken from an anaerobic digester
installed in a WWTP located in CHARGUIA, Tunisia.
Pretreatment Experiments
Coagulation-Flocculation Process
Coagulation-ﬂocculation
experiments
were
carried
at
room temperature using a Floclab Jar Test (Prolabo-France)
equipped with six 500 mL beakers volume. The chemical
reagents used were ferric chloride (FeCl3 .7H2O) as coagu-
lant and polyacrylamide as a ﬂocculant. A 500 mL leachate
sample was poured into each jar. Then, the pH was adjusted
to the desired value using 1 M HCl or 5 M NaOH. Hydro-
chloride acid, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen peroxide
were purchased from Merck (France). The experimental pro-
cess consisted of three subsequent phases according to
Smaoui et al. [18]. A ﬂash mixing started at 150 rpm and
lasted 4.5 min during the coagulant addition. The ﬂoccula-
tion process was conducted for 60 min by slow stirring at a
speed of 48 rpm. After that, a decantation time of 30 min
was performed. Samples were taken from the liquid level
about 3 cm below the surface for chemical analyses.
Fenton Oxidation Process
The iron metal used in this study was obtained from a
metal turner and was added to the leachate solution. Then,
hydrogen peroxide was introduced to start the Fenton reac-
tion while a continuous stirring at 200 rpm was applied. The
chain reaction in the Fenton process is shown in Eqs. 1–5
[19].

To ﬁnish the production of OH radicals and to remove resid-
ual hydrogen peroxide, pH of the samples were brought to
more than 10 using 10 M NaOH [21].
Air Stripping Process
Design of Experiments
The air stripping process was designed and optimized
using RSM. The experimental design and optimization were
conducted with NEMROD W software. A Central Composite
Design (CCD) was used for three variables and three levels,
to optimize three factors i.e. pH, aeration rate and reaction
time as the main factors of the air stripping process. The
ranges and the levels of the variables investigated in this
study are given in Table 2. The range of pH values selected
was based on the best performance of the application. The
aeration rates were chosen to avoid evaporation problems.
The reaction time was chosen on the basis of preliminary
experiments.

Air Stripping Experiments
Two liters of LFL were pured in the air stripping unit,
which consisted of a Plexiglas column. The experimental
conditions are indicated in Table 3. Air charged with ammo-
nia was released through the top of the stripping column.
The (NH4-N) supernatant was measured and the optimal
conditions for the removal of most ammonia determined.
Batch Anaerobic Digestion
Batch anaerobic digestion was conducted to further exam-
ine the effect of each pretreatment studied on biogas produc-
tion. These experiments were carried out under mesophilic
conditions (37 6 18C) for 50 days, using 500 mL glass bottles as
reactors. Each bottle was fed with an appropriate amount of
substrate and inocula, keeping a volatile solids (VS) ratio (VSs
to VSi) at 1:1 in all setups [22]. Five experiments bottles were
performed. They contain: anaerobic sludge without LFL, anaer-
obic sludge with raw LFL, anaerobic sludge with LFL treated by
coagulation-ﬂocculation, anaerobic sludge with LFL treated by
FO and anaerobic sludge with LFL treated by air stripping. The
control batch was conducted only with inocula, to estimate the
volume of biogas resulting from the auto-fermentation of the
inocula biomass. The pH of the leachate samples was adjusted
to 7.0. All bottles were purged with a gas mixture of 75% N2
and 25% CO2 for 3–4 min to supply anaerobic conditions. The
volume of the produced biogas was monitored daily by the dis-
placement method, and the water and corresponding biogas
volumes were calculated. The direct measurement of the meth-
ane produced was carried out using an alkaline solution 5%
(w/v) instead of water, which effectively absorbs all the
content of CO2 in the off-gas [23]. All results are presented as
averages of duplicates with standard deviation.
Analytical Methods
The physico-chemical analysis of leachate samples was
performed according to American Standard Methods for
Water and Wastewater Examination [24].
The pH of the solution was determined using a pH meter
(Metrohm). The electrical conductivity was measured by
WTW Multiline 3410 devices. The chemical oxygen demand
(COD) values were determined by titration after a total
digestion with H2SO4 and potassium dichromate at 1508C for
2h [2]. The biological oxygen demand (BOD5) value was
determined
by
the
respirometric
method
using
WTW
OxiTop. The total Kjeldahl nitrogen content (TKN) and the
ammoniacal nitrogen (NH4-N) were analyzed as a Kjeldahl-N
method. The total concentrations of Fe, Ni, Cr, Pb, Cd, and
Zn were determined using atomic absorption ﬂame emission
spectroscopy AAS (Thermo Scientiﬁc).
Statistical Analysis
All the results were expressed as a mean 6 standard devi-
ation, and the statistical evaluation was performed using
one-way ANOVA (analysis of variance) method followed by
post hoc Tukey’s test with a 0.05 signiﬁcance level to deter-
mine whether the different pretreatments were statistically
different from each other or not.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Physico-Chemical Characterization
As a ﬁrst step, it is important to determine the physico-
chemical characteristics of the leachate used in this study.
The analytical data are presented in Table 1. The leachate
samples are characterized by alkaline pH ranging from 8 to
8.2 with a dark brown color, which indicate the high pres-
ence of humic substances [25], a high electrical conductivity
(EC 5 36.8 mS/cm), a high organic load expressed in COD
with a mean value of 40 g/L and a BOD5/COD ratio of 0.27
indicating the low biodegradability of the leachate. The
Nitrogen concentration was also high mainly in ammonium.
This is correlated with what was reported in the literature
[26]. The NH4-N present in the solution is an essential nutri-
ent for anaerobic bacteria, but it became toxic and consti-
tuted an inhibitor for the anaerobic treatment at high
concentration [27,28]. It’s apparent from Table 1 that leachate
metal contents are low; nevertheless, some micro-pollutant
minerals such as iron and chrome are also present.
Coagulation-Flocculation Pretreatment
The ﬁrst step was to search for the optimum pH of the
coagulation-ﬂocculation process. Therefore an optimization
was carried out by following the evolution of COD removal
at different pH ranging from 3 to 7 (Figure 1a). It was
observed that COD removal from leachate at pH 7 was 35%.
However, an improvement of the results was obtained by

decreasing the pH value and the most signiﬁcant COD
removal occurred at pH 4. In fact, the increase of the solu-
tion pH resulted in a reduction in the retention of ferric chlo-
ride particles. This can be explained by the pH effect on the
nature of produced polymeric metal species that will be
formed as soon as the metal coagulants are dissolved in
water. According to Li et al. [29], the removal efﬁciency is
better at acidic than the basic condition and this can be due
to the different hydrolyzed species of ferric ion. Maranon
et al. [30] suggested that pH 3.8 was considered as the opti-
mum condition for this process. On the other hand, Guer-
reiro et al. [4] showed that the best removal of COD and
BOD5 was obtained at pH 3. At this pH, the coagulation-
ﬂocculation occurs probably by a mechanism of charge neu-
tralization [31]. In fact, we note that the extent of pH range is
affected by different factors, such as the types of coagulant
used, the chemical composition of wastewater and the con-
centration of coagulant. To optimize the COD removal, the
concentration of Fe21 was progressively varied from 0.2 to
1 g/L at pH 4 (Figure 1b). The optimal COD removal of 46%
was obtained at a concentration of Fe0 equal to 0.8 g/L.
Above this dose, no further COD removal was observed. The
overdose of coagulant resulted in the absorbance of the cati-
ons by colloids, which become positively charged and led to
an electronic repulsion and decreased the capacity of organic
matter removal [11]. Others studies have proven that the
addition of coagulants such as Fe21 resulted in the increase
of COD removal which is associated with the decrease of
humic substances [32].
Optimization of the Fenton Process
An optimum oxidation can be obtained if the consumption
of hydroxyl radicals by the reagents is limited. This implies that
neither hydrogen peroxide nor ferrous ions should overdose,
so the ratio [H2O2]/[Fe21] should be optimized to obtain the
maximum amount of hydroxyl radicals and after that oxidize
organic pollutants. Experiments involving H2O2 doses within
the range of 0 - 4 g/L were carried out at pH 3 using 1 g/L of
Fe0. As shown (Figure 2a), the increase of H2O2 concentration
had a positive effect on COD removal. Thus, optimal COD
removal of 30% was obtained at 3 g/L H2O2. The further
increase of H2O2 concentration did not increase the COD
removal efﬁciency. This can be explained by the saturation of
the oxidation process [33]. This result was also found in other
studies which explained this phenomenon by the auto-
decomposition of H2O2 to oxygen and water, and the recombi-
nation of OH• radicals [34]. The COD removal increased gradu-
ally with increasing Fe0 and reached 44% at 2 g/L of metallic

concentration, COD removal decreased and remained steady.
From the reaction, the degradation of organic matter is slow
because of the small production of iron II. After that, the con-
centration of iron increased interactions with hydroxyl radicals,
which causes the maximum removal of COD and the dark
color becomes brown. The overdose of Fe21 or H2O2 can react
with the hydroxyl radical and inhibits the oxidation reaction
[20]. In comparison with other studies, Mohajeri et al. [34] were
observed a COD reduction of 58% with H2O2 and Fe21 concen-
trations of 0.033 mol/L and 0.011 mol/L, respectively. Lopez
et al. [35] observed a 60% COD removal by using reagent dos-
ages as high as 10,000 mg/L of H2O2 and 830 mg/L of Fe21
within 2 h. Boumechour et al. [36] proved that the maximum
COD removal (64%) was achieved by using the optimum
operational conditions of 4 g/L H2O2 and 1 g/L Fe21.
Optimization of the Air Stripping Process
Model Equation and Validation
The
optimization
of
the
experimental
conditions
of
ammonia removal was achieved using a CCD design and car-
ried out under several experimental conditions including pH,
aeration rate and reaction time. The results of the variance
analysis for the ﬁtted model are summarized in Table 3. The
regression sum of square is statistically signiﬁcant at the level
99.9%. Moreover, the coefﬁcient of determination R2 was
0.978; this means that 97.8% of the observed variations of
the response are attributed to the variable effects, and the
experimental values are in excellent agreement with the pre-
dicted values of the reply. This reveals the high validity and
the proper ﬁtting of the model obtained for ammonia
removal. On the other hand, a comparison between the vari-
ance related to the lack of ﬁt to that of pure error has been
established and the results show the nonsigniﬁcance of the
lack of ﬁt (Table 4). The model obtained was used to predict
response values in the domain studied and to draw isores-
ponse contour plots and response surfaces.
Interpretation of the Response Surface Model
Ridge Analysis
The representation of the optimum path for the analysis
of the removal of the ammonia by the response surface is
shown in Figure 3. The method consists in plotting the
curves in order to determine the maximum values of the
response. The left and right parts of both plots indicate the
minimization and the maximization of the response, respec-
tively. Figure 3a shows that the maximum ammonia removal
increased from the center to the boundary. Figure 3b dis-
plays the coordinates for each factor, in codiﬁed variables. It
can be seen that maximum ammonia removal is obtained by
adjustment of all the factors to a high value.

revealing ways of illustrating and interpreting the response
surface system. They are used to evaluate the inﬂuence of

Figure 4a shows the high interaction between pH and
aeration rate. Indeed, ammonia removal increased with the
simultaneous rising of both factors. However, when the pH
was less than 10.5, the phenomenon was primarily governed
by the rate of the aeration factor. Beyond this value, the pH
became predominant. To maximize the response, we must
increase both the pH and the aeration rate. Figure 4b
represented the isocontour plot when the level of the aera-
tion rate was ﬁxed at 7 L/min. It’s clear that yields higher
than 85% could be reached by ﬁxing the pH at 12 and reac-
tion time at 18 h. These results are in agreement with those
of Guo et al. [37] who obtained a removal of 96.6% of
ammonia at pH 11.0 and an aeration time of 18 h. Similarly,
Marttinen et al. [25] have shown a removal of 89% at pH 11
and aeration time of 24h. Finally, it can be seen in Figure 4c,

COD, BOD, and NH4 Reductions Obtained in Each
Pretreatment Step
The COD, BOD and ammonia reduction obtained after
the coagulation-ﬂocculation, Fenton’s oxidation and air strip-
ping pretreatments are presented in Table 5. An improve-
ment of leachate biodegradability after all the pretreatments
applied
was
observed.
Therefore,
the
BOD/COD
ratio
increased from 0.28 to 0.32, to 0.37 and 0.39 for air stripping,
coagulation- ﬂocculation and FO respectively.
Therefore, FO and coagulation- ﬂocculation exhibited a
high performance to remove organic matter and thus, to
enhance the biodegradability of the efﬂuent. In addition, the
zero valent iron used during FO treatment is cheap and non-
toxic. In spite of the mentioned advantages, these two tech-
niques present some drawbacks like the low ammonia
reduction (Table 5), low pH requirement and the generation
of sludge [19]. After, applying the tested pretreatment pro-
cess, LFL can be classiﬁed as a biodegradable efﬂuent and,
thus, the anaerobic digestion can be carried out [38]. These
results are in agreement with Ghanbari et al. [39] who
showed a biodegradability improvement from 0.11 to 0.24
and 0.4 after pretreatment of LFL with coagulation and Fen-
ton process. Lopez et al. [35] observed that Fenton process
could be useful to improve the biodegradability of leachate
that can be treated in a subsequent biological reactor. Vilar
et al. [40] have shown a removal of organic matter and an
increase of the biodegradability after FO of leachate. Com-
pared to other treatments, the air stripping leads to high
ammonia removal, which is an inhibitor of the anaerobic
digestion [7], and therefore improves the C/N ratio (Table 5).
Nevertheless, this process presents the necessity of a high
pH value [41].

CONCLUSION
This study investigated the effect of coagulation–ﬂoccula-
tion, Fenton oxidation and air stripping pretreatments on the
improvement of LFL anaerobic digestion. For each pretreat-
ment, the operational conditions are optimized.
In the case of coagulation-ﬂocculation, a 46 and 18% of
COD and ammonia removal were obtained respectively by
adjusting the pH to 4 and FeCl3 to 0.8 g/L. The BOD/COD
ratio was increased from 0.3 to 0.37.
Under optimum conditions of FO (pH 5 3, Fe052 g/L and
3 g/L [H2O2]), the BOD/COD ratio increased from 0.3 to 0.39
and the ammonia removal was 23%.
Ammonia air stripping at its optimum operating condi-
tions (pH 511, aeration rate 57 L/min and 18 h) achieved
over 85% ammonia and 26% COD removal.
A comparison of three different pretreatment methods of
LFL for biogas production was performed in batch condition.
The methane production was improved for all the pretreated
leachate when compared to the raw LFL.
After anaerobic digestion, the best methane yield using
